title: Five questions to answer before entering a new export market
summary: Expanding into a new country is one of the most rewarding moves a growing business can make — and one of the easiest to get wrong. Start with these five questions.
description:
Expanding into a new country is one of the most rewarding moves a growing business can make — and one of the easiest to get wrong. Before committing budget, it pays to answer five simple questions honestly.

## 1. Is there real demand for what we sell?

Look beyond headline market size. Speak to potential buyers, distributors and importers, and test whether your product solves a problem they recognise, at a price they will pay.

## 2. What will it take to comply?

Product standards, labelling, registrations and import rules vary by market and by product. Map them early with qualified local advisers so there are no surprises at the border.

## 3. Who will we partner with?

Most successful market entries rely on a local partner — a distributor, agent or joint-venture partner who understands the market. Define what a good partner looks like before you start searching.

> The right partner can open a market faster than any campaign.

## 4. Can our supply chain deliver?

Consider lead times, shipping modes, landed costs and how you will handle returns or after-sales service. A plan that works for one container a quarter may not work for one a week.

## 5. How will we measure success?

Agree clear milestones — first orders, repeat orders, margin targets — and a point at which you will review, adjust or step back.

Answering these questions does not remove risk, but it turns a leap into a series of informed steps.

title: Incoterms in plain language: who pays, and who is responsible
summary: Incoterms® rules define how costs and risks are shared between buyer and seller. A quick guide to four of the most common.
description:
Incoterms® rules, published by the International Chamber of Commerce, define how costs and risks are shared between buyer and seller in international trade. Choosing the right one up front avoids disputes later.

## Why they matter

An Incoterm tells both parties who arranges transport, who pays for it and at which point risk passes from seller to buyer. It does not cover payment terms or transfer of ownership — those belong elsewhere in your contract.

## Four terms you will see often

- EXW (Ex Works) — the buyer takes on almost all costs and risks from the seller’s premises.
- FOB (Free On Board) — used for sea freight; risk passes once the goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment.
- CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) — the seller pays freight and minimum insurance to the destination port, but risk passes when the goods are loaded.
- DAP (Delivered at Place) — the seller delivers to a named place, ready for unloading; the buyer handles import clearance.

Always state the Incoterms edition and the exact named place in your contract, and take professional advice for complex shipments.

title: Building a resilient supply chain: a practical checklist
summary: Disruption is a normal part of global trade. Resilience is about being ready for it — here is where to start.
description:
Disruptions — from port congestion to sudden demand spikes — are a normal part of global trade. Resilience is not about predicting every problem; it is about being ready to respond.

## A practical checklist

- Map your critical suppliers and identify single points of failure.
- Qualify at least one alternative source for key inputs.
- Hold safety stock where lead times are long or unpredictable.
- Agree clear communication routines with logistics partners.
- Review routes and modes regularly, not only when something goes wrong.

> Resilience is built before the disruption, not during it.

## Start small

You do not need to redesign everything at once. Begin with the products that matter most to your customers and your margins, then extend the approach.

title: What makes a cross-border partnership last
summary: Most international partnerships begin with enthusiasm. The ones that last are built on clarity.
description:
Most international partnerships begin with enthusiasm. The ones that last are built on clarity — about goals, roles and what happens when things do not go to plan.

## Agree what success looks like

Set shared targets for the first year: volumes, markets, service levels. Revisit them together rather than measuring each other privately.

## Communicate more than you think you need to

Time zones, languages and business cultures all add friction. Regular, structured check-ins prevent small misunderstandings from becoming big ones.

> Trust is built in small, consistent actions over time.

## Share the upside — and the problems

Partners who share good news and bad news early tend to solve problems faster and stay together longer.

title: Preparing your business for investment conversations
summary: Investors look for clarity: a clear opportunity, a credible team and reliable information. Here is how to prepare.
description:
Investors look for clarity: a clear opportunity, a credible team and reliable information. Preparing well shortens conversations and builds confidence.

## Get your information in order

- Up-to-date financial statements
- A concise business plan with realistic assumptions
- Clear ownership and legal documents
- An honest view of key risks and how you manage them

## Know what you are asking for

Be specific about how much investment you are seeking, what it will be used for and what you are prepared to offer in return.

This article is general information, not financial or legal advice. Always consult licensed professionals before entering into an investment agreement.

title: Sea or air freight? Choosing the right mode for your shipment
summary: The choice usually comes down to time, cost and the nature of the goods. Here is how to weigh them up.
description:
The choice between sea and air freight usually comes down to three things: how quickly the goods are needed, what you can afford to spend and what you are shipping.

## When sea freight makes sense

Large volumes, heavy goods and shipments that are not urgent. Sea freight generally costs less per unit but takes considerably longer.

## When air freight makes sense

Urgent, high-value, perishable or smaller consignments. Air freight is faster but more expensive, so it is often reserved for goods where speed protects value.

## Consider the whole journey

Door-to-door time includes collection, port or airport handling, customs clearance and final delivery — not just time in transit.

title: Documentation basics for first-time importers
summary: Paperwork is where many first shipments slow down. Knowing the common documents helps you prepare.
description:
Paperwork is where many first shipments slow down. Knowing the documents you are likely to need — and who provides them — helps everything move faster.

## Common documents

- Commercial invoice
- Packing list
- Bill of lading (sea) or air waybill (air)
- Certificate of origin, where required
- Product-specific permits, licences or certificates

Requirements vary by product and by country. Always confirm the latest rules with a licensed customs broker before goods are shipped.
